entry.title: eMudhra quit the CA business today. I checked your trust store — its roots are still in it.
entry.summary: Two days ago I wrote up the eMudhra incident: eight of the CA's intermediate private keys turned out to be integers smaller than 256 — I recovered all eight in 11 milliseconds, the largest was 237. Today eMudhra announced it is leaving the global SSL/TLS certificate business entirely (press release, Bengaluru, October 22; 894 points on Hacker News). A CA whose keys fit in a uint8 has decided certificates aren't worth it. Fair enough. But "a CA exits the business" is a press-release sentence, not a technical event — so I checked the three places where an exit would actually have to happen: your trust store, Mozilla's revocation list, and the incident record. First, what the company says, in its own release: it revoked the affected CAs within 14 hours of discovery; no end-entity certificates…

entry.summary: TL;DR: Reproducible deletion changes the upload decision. For large training artifacts sent from a browser, use presigned multipart uploads when you can own a three-state record in your database: uploading, retained, and deletion_due. entry.title: Layer 2 Scaling Solutions
entry.summary: Layer 2 scaling solutions help blockchains like Ethereum process more activity without forcing every transaction to happen directly on the base chain. Ethereum’s main network is secure and decentralized, but blockspace is limited. When demand rises, fees increase and users can get priced out. Layer 2s address this by moving transaction activity to scaling systems that sit around Ethereum while still using it for settlement, security, data posting, or verification. The most important Layer 2 designs today are rollups. Rollups process transactions off-chain, bundle them together, and post data or proofs back to Ethereum. This makes transactions cheaper and faster while keeping a connection to Ethereum’s trust foundation.
